newsitem.title: KENYA: Scant success for strike, protests in Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Scant success for strike, protests in Kenya.

text.p: A national strike and protest marches called by Kenyan opposition leaders had scant success on Friday and the battered currency recouped some of its losses.
Barely 1,000 activists turned up in Nairobi's Uhuru park to hear opposition speakers demand sweeping political reforms from President Daniel arap Moi before elections due this year.

Most city centre shops were closed and some workers stayed at home. But shop-owners, many from the vulnerable Asian community, said they closed for fear of the violence and looting which mar political demonstrations in Kenya.
Moi's government declared the strike and planned rallies unlawful but security forces allowed the Nairobi meeting to go ahead without disruption.
The port of Mombasa, the East African country's second city, was calm with only a few shops closed, residents said.
Tension has risen steadily in the past two months and at least nine people were killed on July 7 when security forces suppressed pro-reform protests in Nairobi and other centres.
The shilling sank to an historic official low against the dollar on Thursday but regained 1.85 percent by about midday on Friday, standing at a commercial mean of 68.06 to the dollar.

But traders said the currency was still fragile and it was too soon to talk of a recovery. The shilling has still lost nearly 16 percent since the International Monetary Fund (IMF) shelved a $205 million loan last week because of concerns over official corruption.
Now aged 73 and in power since 1978, Moi wants a final five-year term. Under pressure at home and from Western donors, he has assented to some reforms before the polls.
This concession has successfully deepened the divisions within the opposition and two prominent leaders, Kenneth Matiba and Kijana Wamalwa, opposed Friday's strike.
Work went on almost as normal in Nairobi's industrial area, one employer said.
"We are open. Almost everybody -- about 180 of my 200 employees -- turned up," bed and mattress manufacturer Mahedi Meghji told Reuters.
By early afternoon the worst incidents were in Nairobi's vast Mathare slum where unemployed youths set barricades of burning tyres and clashed with riot police.
Chanting "Moi must go" they attacked a bar because it stayed open and looted iron sheets.

They tried to join the rally in the park but were barred from marching through the Eastleigh suburb by ethnic Somalis living there. Somalis told Reuters they were not opposed by reforms but rejected the pattern of looting and violence during such protests.
In the park, speeches by Raila Odinga and other opposition leaders were punctuated by cries of "No reforms, no elections".
Speakers were at times ignored as groups of young men picked on those they said were police spies, beating them with fists, kicks and belts.
Strike advocates won no support in Friday's newspapers including the independent Daily Nation.
"The strike which has been called for today is not the best method of pressing home the need for constitutional reform," the Nation said in an editorial.
It said workers who stayed at home were as likely to be fearful for their security as showing support for the strike.

The strike and marches in Nairobi and 11 provincial towns were called by the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC), an umbrella reform group which wants sweeping changes to the constitution and the repeal of numerous laws before the elections.
